turns.doctor_question: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Hi, Doctor. Nice to meet you. Well, it's... it's a bit embarrassing to admit at my age, honestly. I'm forty-nine, and I feel like I should really have a handle on myself by now, but what brings me in is that I just keep getting up when I'm supposed to stay put. 

I'm a private investigator, which, you know, sounds very action-packed on television, but in reality, a huge part of the job is just sitting. Sitting in cars for surveillance, sitting across a desk from clients who are usually incredibly stressed out. And lately, right in the middle of these heavy client interviews, I just... I keep standing up. A client will be pouring their heart out about a cheating spouse or a missing business asset, and I'll just abruptly pop out of my chair. I'll start pacing, or I'll walk over to the window, or I'll make up an excuse to check the coffee maker. It's terribly unprofessional. 

And it's not even just at work! I do some tutoring on the side, and I can't even sit next to a student to go over their algebra without suddenly needing to stand up and walk around the room. Even at my Wednesday night book club—which is supposed to be relaxing, we're reading historical fiction right now, usually over a glass of wine—I'm the only one who can't just sit on the sofa. I'm up and down, up and down. People are really starting to notice, and I'm getting these looks from my friends and my clients because it seems like I can't just sit and listen to them. I *want* to listen, I really do, but I just can't seem to stay in the chair. It's starting to affect my reputation, and I just don't know why I'm doing it.

symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient explicitly describes repeatedly leaving their seat during situations where they are expected to remain seated, such as client interviews, tutoring sessions, and book club.

turns.doctor_question: When you feel that urge to stand up and move around, do you experience an inner feeling of restlessness or tension in your body that makes it uncomfortable to stay seated, or does it feel more like an automatic habit or impulse that just happens?
turns.patient_response:
You know, I... I've never really stopped to think about it in those exact terms. That's a very perceptive question, but I honestly couldn't tell you. I mean, if I try to put myself back in one of those moments to figure it out—like, just last Thursday, for example. I was doing this surveillance job out in the suburbs, sitting in my sedan for about four hours watching this house. The neighborhood was so quiet, just sprinklers going off, and I was trying to stay completely still so I wouldn't draw attention to the car. 

And then suddenly, I'm just getting out of the car. But was it a physical tension beforehand? Like a tightness in my muscles or an ache? I'm really not sure. I haven't noticed anything like that. I don't think my body physically hurts or feels tight. 

But then, on the other hand, is it just an automatic habit? I don't really know that either, because it doesn't feel like a routine I've just gotten used to, if that makes sense. It’s like... one minute I’m sitting across from a client, looking right at their paperwork—usually financial disclosures, which are incredibly dry and take hours to comb through, just pages and pages of bank statements—and the next minute I'm on my feet walking to the water cooler. I just haven't paid close enough attention to the exact second right before I stand up to know if my body feels uncomfortable or if my brain just flips a switch without me realizing it. I've been so focused on how embarrassed I am *after* I stand up, especially when I catch my book club friends giving each other *that* look, that I haven't really analyzed the feeling right before it happens. I wish I could give you a better answer, I really do, but I just don't know.

symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient describes multiple instances of unexpectedly leaving their seat when they are expected to remain seated, such as during a surveillance job, while reviewing paperwork with a client, and at a book club.
symptom_reasoning.S061: The patient explicitly states that they do not think their body physically hurts or feels tight, denying muscle tension.

turns.doctor_question: When you stand up and start moving around, does it feel like you *have* to do it—like there's an uncomfortable sensation that forces you to move—or could you physically stay seated if you really tried hard, even though you don't want to?
turns.patient_response:
Well, gosh, could I stay seated if I tried really hard... I mean, I feel like I *do* try hard! I really do. But I just don't know if I could physically force myself to stay put, because... well, let me give you an example. 

Just last Tuesday, I had this new client, Mrs. Gable. Older woman, very proper, wearing this immaculate tweed suit, paying me a very good retainer to look into her son-in-law's business dealings. Before she even walked into my office, I gave myself a whole pep talk. I stood by the door and said out loud to myself, 'Do not stand up today. Just sit there, be professional, and listen to her.' I went and sat down, I had my yellow legal pad perfectly aligned on the desk, my favorite pen ready, I even tucked my feet all the way under my desk chair—it's one of those heavy leather swivel chairs—just so I wouldn't be able to easily use my legs to push off the floor. I was really preparing myself to just stay anchored.

And for the first twenty minutes, it was fine. She was explaining all these complicated shell companies, which is tedious but very important for the investigation, and I was sitting. But then... well, I don't know if I *could* have stopped myself when it finally happened, because honestly, I didn't even realize I was doing it until I was already halfway across the room adjusting the window blinds. So, did I try hard enough? I thought I was trying! 

But as to whether there's an uncomfortable sensation forcing me out of the chair... I just can't say for sure. I don't think so? It's not like a pain or a burning feeling or a cramp that makes me jump up to relieve it. But then again, if I really, really focused every single ounce of my brainpower on just gluing myself to the chair, maybe I could stay down? But then I wouldn't be listening to the client at all, would I? I'd just be sitting there agonizing over the act of sitting. So I really couldn't tell you if it's a physical impossibility or just... I don't know, a failure of my own willpower. I wish I could give you a simple yes or no about what exactly is driving it, but I just don't know.

symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient describes a specific instance where she unintentionally left her seat during a professional meeting despite making a strong effort to remain seated.

turns.doctor_question: When you're sitting in those situations—with your client, at book club, during tutoring—and you feel that urge to stand up and move around, are you also experiencing any racing thoughts, worry, or a sense of anxiety or nervousness at that same moment, or is your mind relatively calm?
turns.patient_response:
You know, that's actually the strange part. You'd think I'd be a nervous wreck or something, right? But no, I don't feel anxious at all. I mean... I really don't think my mind is racing with worry when it happens. 

Take my tutoring, for instance. I help this lovely kid, Kevin, he's a freshman, great kid but his handwriting is just atrocious, completely illegible. We were sitting at his parents' kitchen table on Monday—they have this huge, beautiful oak table, very sturdy, you know the kind that takes four people to move—and we were going over polynomials. I wasn't worried about anything. I wasn't stressed. I was literally just looking at this equation, trying to figure out how to explain factoring to him in a way that wouldn't make his eyes glaze over, because algebra is so dry if you don't connect it to something real. My mind was completely focused on the math. It was totally calm, no racing thoughts, no panic. And yet, right in the middle of explaining the difference between a coefficient and a constant, I just... popped up and walked over to their refrigerator to look at a magnet. I wasn't anxious! I just did it.

And it's the exact same thing at book club. We were at my friend Susan's house this past week. She always hosts the third Wednesday of the month and makes these incredible charcuterie boards, I mean, she really goes all out with the little fig jams and the artisanal cheeses, it's lovely. We were discussing the chapters, sipping a very nice Pinot Noir, and I was perfectly relaxed. I mean, these are women I've known for almost a decade, there is absolutely zero reason for me to be nervous or on edge around them. My mind wasn't racing with worry at all. We were having a wonderful debate about the main character's choices in the second act, and I was so engaged in the conversation, feeling completely at ease. But then, there I go, standing up and pacing behind the sofa while I'm making my point. 

So, no, I wouldn't say it's a nervous energy or a worried mind at all. I actually feel quite calm mentally in those moments. My thoughts are just on whatever we're doing—the book, the math, the client's file. It's never a sense of panic, which just makes the whole standing up thing even more baffling to me, to be perfectly honest.

symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient explicitly describes leaving their seat during tutoring and book club, such as popping up to look at a refrigerator or pacing behind a sofa.
symptom_reasoning.S038: The patient explicitly denies having racing thoughts, stating their mind is totally calm and focused.
symptom_reasoning.S056: The patient repeatedly denies feeling anxious or worried, stating they are not stressed and do not have a worried mind.
symptom_reasoning.S058: The patient denies feeling nervous or on edge, noting they feel mentally calm and relaxed rather than having nervous energy.

turns.doctor_question: When you're sitting down and get the urge to stand up, do you notice any specific uncomfortable feelings in your legs—like tingling, crawling sensations, aching, or a restless feeling specifically in your legs—or is the urge to move coming from somewhere else entirely?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, tingling? Like... like when your foot falls asleep? No, no, it's definitely not like that. I mean, I know exactly the feeling you're talking about, that sort of pins and needles thing, or like a weird crawling sensation, but I really haven't noticed anything even close to that in my legs. 

Just to be absolutely sure, I'm trying to picture the last time it happened to see if I missed something. Let's see, yesterday afternoon, I was at my office. I actually have this wonderful ergonomic footrest under my desk—I bought it a few years ago because, well, as a private investigator, you spend half your life sitting in completely uncomfortable, cramped cars on stakeouts, so I really wanted my actual office setup to be as supportive and comfortable as humanly possible. So I was sitting there, feet perfectly flat on the footrest, wearing these very comfortable, loose-fitting linen trousers because it was quite warm out, and I was looking through these background checks for a corporate embezzlement case. It's fascinating work, really, seeing how people try to hide assets in plain sight—this one guy had funneled thousands through a fake landscaping company, which I only caught because the billing addresses were actually just empty lots—but it requires a massive amount of cross-referencing. 

Anyway, I was sitting there for maybe forty-five minutes, completely engrossed in these invoices, and my legs felt absolutely fine. No aching, no crawling sensations, no heaviness, no cramps. They weren't bothering me in the slightest. But then, sure enough, I'm suddenly standing up and walking over to the filing cabinet, even though the only file I needed was already wide open right there on my desk! 

So, it's definitely not my legs telling me to move. I don't feel any physical discomfort in my calves or thighs or anything like that right before I stand. The urge just... well, like I said before, I don't even really know where it comes from or how to describe it, but it's certainly not because my legs are uncomfortable or restless. I really wish I could say it was, because then maybe I could just, I don't know, massage my legs or stretch them out a bit and actually manage to stay seated, you know? But no, I haven't noticed any weird feelings in my legs at all.

symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient describes suddenly standing up and walking away from their desk while working, even when they didn't need to retrieve anything.
symptom_reasoning.S015: The patient provides an excessively long and detailed response, going on tangents about their ergonomic footrest, linen trousers, and a corporate embezzlement case just to answer a simple yes/no question.

turns.doctor_question: Besides this difficulty staying seated, do you find it hard to concentrate or focus on tasks, or do you get easily distracted during your investigations and other work? Or do you notice yourself being unusually restless, fidgety, or impulsive in other ways throughout your day?
turns.patient_response:
Well, it's funny you ask about being restless or fidgety in other ways, because even when I do manage to stay in the chair, I am definitely not sitting still. I mean, people think being a private investigator is all glamorous, like you're out in the field wearing a trench coat and taking photos in dark alleys, but honestly? A huge chunk of the job is just grueling, tedious desk work. 

Take last Thursday, for example. I was doing a deep dive into some property deeds and bank statements for this very messy divorce case—the husband was trying to hide a whole condominium in Boca Raton under a dummy corporation, which is just so cliché, honestly, but it still takes hours of digging to prove it. So I'm sitting there, and when I'm stuck at the computer combing through those kinds of records, I am just a ball of motion. My foot will be bouncing up and down under the desk a mile a minute. I don't even realize I'm doing it until my calf actually starts to get tired! 

And my hands, they always have to be doing something too. I always keep a pen nearby—I'm very particular, I only use those Pilot G2 gel pens, the 0.7 millimeter ones in blue ink—and I'll just sit there clicking it. Click, click, click, over and over, sometimes without even noticing until my husband actually has to poke his head into my home office and ask me to please stop making that noise. 

And it's not just the foot bouncing or the pen clicking, either. I'm constantly adjusting how I'm sitting. I'll cross my left leg, then two minutes later uncross it and sit on my right foot, then lean on my left elbow, then slide down a bit, then sit up bone straight. I shift around so much that I actually end up losing my place in what I'm reading! I'll be halfway down a really dense spreadsheet of wire transfers, and I'll squirm around in my seat, and when I look back at the screen, I have absolutely no idea which line I was on. It's incredibly frustrating, because then I have to start the whole column over again just to make sure I didn't miss a transaction. So, yes, even when I'm physically anchored to the desk, I'm definitely still moving around in a hundred different little ways.

symptom_reasoning.S010: The patient explicitly describes bouncing their foot, clicking a pen, and constantly shifting and squirming in their seat while working at their desk.

turns.doctor_question: When did this difficulty with staying seated first start happening? Was this something you've struggled with since you were younger, or is this more of a recent problem that's developed over the past few years?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, goodness, no, this is definitely not a recent thing. If anything, it's basically the story of my life. 

I mean, my mother actually kept all of my old report cards in this big, faded floral shoebox in her hall closet—she's one of those people who saves absolutely everything, every little drawing, every macaroni necklace, you name it—and if you go back and look at those grade-school report cards, it is like reading a broken record. Every single teacher, from Mrs. Gable in second grade all the way up through middle school, they all wrote the exact same thing in the little comments section at the bottom. They'd always say that I was a very bright student, but I just couldn't stay in my seat or wait my turn. Ever! I'd be up at the chalkboard, or over by the class hamster, or just wandering the aisles while everyone else was doing silent reading. 

My mother actually still jokes about it to this day. Especially now that I'm a private investigator, she thinks it's just hilarious. She always says that I was just training for my career early, because I treated every single classroom like a crime scene that I absolutely had to pace through and investigate. She loves telling that story at dinner parties. 

So, yes, to answer your question, this has been happening since I was a little girl. It’s certainly not something that just cropped up over the last few years. I’ve always been the one popping out of my chair when I was supposed to be sitting still, long before I ever had a desk of my own to pace around.

symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient explicitly states they have always had trouble staying in their seat, wandering the aisles, and popping out of their chair when supposed to be sitting still.
symptom_reasoning.S017: The patient mentions that their grade-school report cards noted they could not wait their turn.
